title: Brown cedar (jalnji)

names.gloss: species of poison-nut tree; the gum from it is not poisonous and is used for making spears

identification.basis: Roth's Bloomfield name for the brown-cedar gum, t-chaln-ji, matches the dictionary's jalnji, 'the gum from this tree is used for making spears'. Anderson confirms Canarium australasicum gum for spear points and axe hafts and the blinding smoke of its wood.

summary: **[jalnji](word:jalnji)** is a tree whose 'gum from this tree is not poisonous, used for making spears', and Roth's Bloomfield name for the brown-cedar gum, *t-chaln-ji*, is the same word: this is *Canarium australasicum*, the brown cedar, brown cudgerie or mango bark, the rainforest tree whose dry lumps of gum, baked and pounded, were the cement of the Bloomfield spear and axe [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]. Its bark 'exudes a strong mango odour' when cut, its flowers are dark red to maroon, and its fruit small [ref:rfk-canarium]. Anderson: the stone axe head was set in its lawyer-cane handle with 'a gum mixture of beeswax mixed with resin from *Canarium australasicum*', the stingray barbs on the spears with the same resin, and the harpoon point with 'a ring-plug of gum (usually *Canarium australasicum*)'; and its wood, like the blind-your-eye mangrove's, 'produces a smoke which is said by Kuku-Yalanji to produce blindness' [ref:anderson1996]. At Cape Bedford the tree was also a canoe timber [ref:roth1910]. The gums themselves are on the [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) page.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[jalnji](word:jalnji)** 'species of poison nut tree; gum from this tree is not poisonous, used for making spears' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth: the brown-cedar gum 'is used for fixing together the haft and shaft of spears, and in the old days (R. Hislop) was employed for fixing the stone-celt into its handle. KYE Bld. *t-chaln-ji*. Though the tree is not growing in the immediate vicinity of Cooktown and Cape Bedford, the local (KYI) blacks know the gum as *kun-dar*', and at Cape Bedford the tree itself, as a canoe timber, was *gundar* [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910]. The related **[yikari](word:yikari)** is the traded resin of *Canarium muelleri*, a different tree; the dictionary's cedars **[milbanku](word:milbanku)** and **[mirrbangku](word:mirrbangku)** are the 'pencil cedar' with a sweet date-shaped fruit, and the [red cedar](entry:red-cedar) is *marrakan* [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The tree and the gum
sections.body:
'Brown cudgerie; carrotwood; mango bark; mango carrotwood; parsnip wood': 'freshly cut bark exudes a strong mango odour and a small amount of clear or slightly milky exudate'; the leaves are compound, sometimes reduced on big trees to one leaflet; the flowers 'dark red to maroon' with yellow or orange anthers; the fruits 'about 8–9 mm long' [ref:rfk-canarium].

**The gum.** Roth: 'the dry lumps of gum are gathered off the tree ... and are either wrapped in leaves and baked, or just warmed before a fire, and then pounded between two stones till pliable and soft enough for use' [ref:roth1904]. Anderson: 'the celts were tied onto a handle made of a portion of large lawyer cane and secured there by bark fibre or wallaby sinew and a gum mixture of beeswax mixed with resin from *Canarium australasicum*'; the stingray barbs and prongs 'were held in place by wallaby sinew and resins made from *Canarium australasicum*, *E. chlorostachys* or grasstree'; the harpoon point 'was stuffed into the hollowed-out end of the handle and kept there by a ring-plug of gum (usually *Canarium australasicum*)' [ref:anderson1996]. 'Gums and resins were an important resource ... I have noted the use of *Canarium australasicum* gum for fixing spear points and axe hafts. *C. muelleri* resin, and the gum from a forest Casuarina species, *Xanthorrhoea johnsonii* and *Grevillea striata* were also widely used' [ref:anderson1996].

**The wood.** 'Some wood was very dangerous to use as firewood. For instance, a mangrove species, *Excoecaria agallocha*, produces a smoke which is said by Kuku-Yalanji to produce blindness. This is also true of the "brown cedar", *Canarium australasicum*' [ref:anderson1996]. At Cape Bedford the dug-out canoes were made of '*Canarium australasicum* (KYI *gundar*), and *Gmelina*' [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Brown cedar, red cedar, pencil cedar
sections.body:
- **Brown cedar** (*jalnji*): mango smell from the cut bark, maroon flowers, gum lumps on the trunk; the cement tree [ref:rfk-canarium] [ref:roth1904].
- **[Red cedar](entry:red-cedar)** (*marrakan*): the canoe and timber tree, pinnate leaves, red wood, no mango smell [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Pencil cedar** (*milbanku*, *mirrbangku*): 'the fruit is the shape of a date and very sweet' [ref:hershberger1982].
- ***Canarium muelleri***: the big-teared resin tree of *yikari* [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Dry lumps of gum on the trunk** where the bark has been wounded [ref:roth1904].
- **Mango smell** from a cut in the bark [ref:rfk-canarium].
- **A cassowary or pigeon tree** in fruit in the rainforest [ref:rfk-canarium].
- **Old axe scars** where gum was tapped.

sections.heading: Where it grows
sections.body: A tree of lowland rainforest [ref:rfk-canarium]. It is not found everywhere Kuku Yalanji is spoken: it was not growing near Cooktown, where the gum was known by name but had to be traded in [ref:roth1904]. See each place above for where it grows and where it does not.

sections.heading: The cement tree
sections.body: Brown-cedar gum is the thing that holds the Bloomfield toolkit together: barb to [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera), stone to [axe](entry:axes-and-adzes) haft, point to harpoon, with [beeswax](entry:native-bees) and [sinew](entry:sinew); its wood made the Cape Bedford canoe; and its smoke was the one thing a Bloomfield cook would not have at the fire [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1910]. Gum-cements were among the Bloomfield's trade exports [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Gum lumps are gathered when found and kept, since the cement 'only requires heat to soften it again'; spear and axe work followed the materials, after the storms [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- Spear cement: hafts to shafts, barbs and prongs on the head [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
- Axe cement, mixed with beeswax [ref:anderson1996].
- The harpoon's ring-plug [ref:anderson1996].
- Canoe hulls at Cape Bedford [ref:roth1910].
- Trade: a Bloomfield export [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Preparing the gum
sections.body:
From Roth and Anderson [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Gather the dry lumps of gum from the trunk.
2. Wrap them in leaves and bake them in the ashes, or warm them before the fire.
3. Pound between two stones until soft; at Cooktown the stones were greased with an oily nut so the gum did not stick [ref:roth1904].
4. For an axe, mix with beeswax; work it hot round the binding and let it set [ref:anderson1996].
5. Never burn the wood at the cooking fire [ref:anderson1996].

The whole cement kit is on the [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) page.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- The smoke 'is said by Kuku-Yalanji to produce blindness'; not firewood [ref:anderson1996].
- The dictionary calls it a 'poison nut tree' with a gum that is 'not poisonous'; take the gum and leave the nut [ref:hershberger1982].
- Hot gum burns and sticks.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Whether *jalnji* is this tree exactly is for the people who gather its gum; the contribution box below is for that [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[jalnji](word:jalnji)* the spear-gum tree; *[yikari](word:yikari)* the traded resin; *[milbanku](word:milbanku)*, *[mirrbangku](word:mirrbangku)* 'pencil cedar' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: Brown cedar does not grow on the Hann River. The Atlas of Living Australia has no record of *Canarium australasicum* in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru; the only *Canarium* there is a different tree, *C. australianum* (18 records, 1970–2020), and no source says its gum was used [ref:ala-hann-gums]. The cements of this country were the [ironwood](entry:ironwood) and the [grass tree](entry:grass-tree) [ref:roth1904] [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: **It doesn't.** The brown cedar is a rainforest tree [ref:rfk-canarium], and the Hann is stringybark and bloodwood woodland with a paperbark fringe on the river [ref:wp-hann]. The trees that gave gum here are in the Atlas: ironwood, *Erythrophleum chlorostachys*, 50 records (1970–2026), and the grass tree *Xanthorrhoea johnsonii*, 14 records (1968–2024), in the same box [ref:ala-hann-gums].

sections.heading: The gums people used here
sections.body:
**Ironwood gum.** Roth saw ironwood cement 'in use among the natives of the Endeavour, Laura, and Palmer Rivers, along the Princess Charlotte Bay coast line' about 1900; he noted its 'liability to crack' [ref:roth1904]. See [ironwood](entry:ironwood).

**Grass-tree resin (Kuku Warra, Laura).** A Kuku Warra man from Laura told the Federal Court in 2023: 'At the bottom of the black boy tree, you get a resin right down near the root. You take the root of the tree, cut it with a tomahawk, scrape the dirt off, heat the root on hot coals, and the resin or sap comes out of the root. You can mould the sap to bind things together' [ref:fca-kukuwarra]. Kuku Warra country is around Laura, and it shares the land between the North Kennedy and the Hann with the Thaypan under a customary agreement [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

**Sap, resin and fire (Kuku Thaypan).** The Kuku Thaypan Elders who worked with Standley taught that in their fire knowledge 'weaponry and crafts are intimately tied to fire. Materials used in the creation of weapons require sap and resin and fire is used to stimulate the production of both in species that are utilised for this purpose' [ref:standley2019]. Scarred trees on their country record this: 'Scars can be from harvesting sugarbag (native honey) or resin or for use in tools, weaponry or craft' [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, both determined in November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Scarred trees are part of that country's record; leave them alone [ref:standley2019].

locations.summary: Brown cedar is a long way from [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) on the upper Mitchell; this page is here because the words, the trade and the tools reach inland.

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: Not at Karma Waters, whose cements are the [grass tree](entry:grass-tree), the [ironwood](entry:ironwood) and the spinifex [ref:roth1904].

locations.summary: This is a tree of the sea country of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji, the Bloomfield and Daintree coast, where its gum was the cement of the spear and the axe [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: The lowland rainforest of the Bloomfield and Daintree [ref:rfk-canarium] [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The tree is in the Bloomfield scrubs and its gum still sets a spear; the Eastern Kuku Yalanji country where it grows was handed back to its Traditional Owners in 2021 [ref:handback2021] [ref:anderson1996].
